Filtered Backprojection was implemented by the author of the source material in the context of a personal project to understand tomographic reconstruction [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the author implemented Filtered Backprojection in a personal project to understand tomographic reconstruction. The evidence explicitly states: 'it looks suspiciously like there's a filter in the frequency domain and a reconstruction across all angles' (describing the author's implementation/understanding) and 'I've reinvented filtered back projection'. The context is clearly a personal exploration ('I then headed over to Wikipedia', 'done on this project for now'). Thus, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
supported
The method relies on the linearity of the Radon transform, allowing the filtering and integration steps to be performed in either order [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method relies on the linearity of the Radon transform, allowing filtering and integration to be performed in either order. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'given everything's linear I would expect you could do the integration and filter in either order.' This directly supports the claim regarding the reliance on linearity and the interchangeability of the steps.

The statistical methods look really cool...'. This directly supports the claim that the approach (filtered back projection) is noisier than iterative statistical methods.

Filtered Backprojection (FBP) and Adjoint Methods solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by mapping 2D projection data back into a destination image or volume representation [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that both Filtered Backprojection (FBP) and Adjoint Methods solve the inverse problem. However, the provided evidence (Source [S1]) only discusses 'Filtered Backprojection' (referencing it as 'filtered back projection' and describing the process of filtering and summing across angles). There is no mention of 'Adjoint Methods' in the text. Therefore, the evidence does not support the part of the claim regarding Adjoint Methods.
supported

The passages further discuss 'filtered back projection' and the removal of high frequencies (filtering) to avoid noise, which aligns with the claim.

Unlike unfiltered back-projection which directly scatters data and causes blurring, FBP applies a frequency-domain or spatial-domain filter to the projections before back-projection to correct for this effect [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Filtered Back Projection (FBP) applies a filter to projections before back-projection to correct for blurring/scattering inherent in unfiltered back-projection. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly mentions: 1) 'there's a filter in the frequency domain and a reconstruction across all angles', 2) 'the filter is applied before the summing across all angles' (where summing across angles is the back-projection step), and 3) 'removal of the high frequencies to avoid noise' and 'deconvolution due to attenuated frequencies' (which explains the correction for the blurring/attenuation effect). The source confirms the order of operations (filter before back-projection) and the purpose (deconvolution/correction).
